title: Strangers
tomorrow: the rich man in the story has no name. why does the poor man?

cards: A knock at nine at night. You check the doorbell camera before you move. A face you don't know.

So, what if the stranger at your door is an angel? The letter to the Hebrews says it straight, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "hospitality do not forget; for by this some, being not aware of it, have entertained angels."
The King James Bible says some have "entertained angels unawares." And yet you still checked the camera. Inside the Catholic tradition, both of those instincts have a voice.

teach.b: First voice: welcome, wide open. Genesis tells of Abraham at his tent door in the heat of the day. Three strangers appear, and he runs to meet them, bows, and hurries to bake bread.
He doesn't know yet who they are.

Jesus raises the stakes in Matthew: "I was a stranger, and you took me in." Saint Benedict's Rule tells monks to receive every guest as Christ himself. On this view, the stranger is never a risk first.
Second voice: prudence. The Catechism calls prudence the virtue that helps you see the true good in each situation and choose the right way to reach it.
A parent who tells a child not to open the door at night isn't failing at love.
Someone responsible for others has to weigh the welcome against their safety, and the Church counts that weighing as a virtue, not a lack of faith.
Hold both, and you get a question, not a rule: how do I welcome well, here, tonight? And under both voices sits one thing they share.
Paul tells the Athenians that God made all mankind of one, to dwell on the face of the earth.
The Second Vatican Council said the same: all peoples form one community, with one origin. The stranger is never a different kind of human. Just one you haven't met.

how: Catholics count welcoming the stranger among the works of mercy, from Matthew 25, and the Rule of Saint Benedict asks monasteries to receive every guest as Christ.

practice: If you can, walk slowly to your front door, or picture it, and rest a hand on it. Think of the people who have come through it, the welcome ones and the unexpected ones.
Then think of one stranger you'll likely pass this week, and decide on one kind word you could give them.
